title: YOUR BODY IS NOT YOURS
paragraphs:
YOUR BODY IS NOT YOURS
What “The Temple of the Holy Spirit” Really Demands From Christians—and Why Grace Will Not Leave You Where It Found You
There is a sentence in the Bible Christians quote when someone gets a tattoo.
Or drinks too much.
Or eats badly.
Or smokes.
Or neglects exercise.
“Don’t you know your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit?”
Sometimes the person saying it means well.
Sometimes the verse is being used like a religious hammer.
And sometimes we have repeated the sentence so often that we have stopped hearing how absolutely staggering it actually is.
Because when Paul wrote those words, he was dealing with something far deeper than a Christian wellness program.
He was confronting believers who were trying to separate what they did with their bodies from whom they belonged to spiritually.
And Paul’s answer was devastating.
You cannot give Jesus your “soul” while reserving your body for yourself.
You cannot call Christ Lord and then quietly place a sign over your physical life that says:
PRIVATE PROPERTY.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because the actual text says something many modern Christians would rather soften.
Paul writes:
The heart of 1 Corinthians 6:19 is astonishing:
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you... and you are not your own.”
Not your own.
Three words that collide violently with almost everything our culture teaches us.
“My body. My choice.”
“My desires. My rules.”
“My private life.”
“Nobody gets to tell me what I do with myself.”
Then the Gospel walks into the room and says something radically different.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, you have been redeemed at a price.
Paul continues:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.”
“For you were bought with a price.”
And then comes the command:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
That changes everything.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “Despise your body.”
He does not say, “Your body is dirty.”
He does not say, “Punish yourself until God accepts you.”
He says your body belongs to the One who purchased you.
And what was the price?
Not money.
Not religious performance.
Not your promise to become a better person.
Peter describes our redemption with breathtaking clarity: we were not redeemed with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with “the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Your body matters because the cross says you matter.
Christianity is not the story of escaping physical existence so our souls can float somewhere spiritual.
The Christian Gospel is scandalously embodied.
The Son of God took on flesh.
Jesus hungered.
Jesus became tired.
Jesus wept.
Jesus bled.
Jesus was crucified bodily.
Jesus was buried bodily.
And Jesus rose bodily.
The Christian hope itself includes “the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23).
So when Scripture talks about your body, it is talking about something God created, Christ purchased, the Spirit indwells, and God ultimately intends to redeem.
That means the question is much larger than:
“Can Christians do this?”
“Can Christians drink that?”
“Can Christians wear this?”
“Can Christians get that tattoo?”
“Can Christians eat this food?”
Those questions may sometimes matter.
But there is a deeper question underneath all of them:
Can I glorify Jesus Christ with what I am about to do with the body He purchased?
And suddenly the hiding places begin disappearing.
Because 1 Corinthians 6 was written into a real moral crisis.
Corinth was a world where sexual immorality was hardly shocking. Paul confronts believers who apparently believed sexual behavior could be treated almost like satisfying another bodily appetite.
His response is uncompromising:
“The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” (1 Corinthians 6:13).
Then he goes further.
Our bodies are members of Christ.
That is the immediate context Christians must not erase.
When Paul says your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, he is not primarily handing the Corinthians a fitness slogan.
He is confronting sexual immorality and declaring that union with Christ changes what believers may do with their bodies.
The Greek word translated “temple” is ναός — naos.
That matters.
Paul could speak of a broader temple complex using other terminology, but naos commonly refers to the sanctuary itself—the sacred dwelling place associated with God's presence.
Think about the weight of that imagery.
Under the old covenant, God's holy presence was associated uniquely with the sanctuary.
Now Paul looks at ordinary Christians—flawed Christians, tempted Christians, Christians with histories they probably wished they could erase—and says:
The Holy Spirit is in you.
Not because you became impressive.
Because you belong to Christ.
That should produce wonder before it produces rules.
But wonder eventually demands surrender.
And this is where some of us need to stop reading for thirty seconds and become painfully honest.
What have you been doing with the body that belongs to Jesus?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your browser history knows.
Maybe the person whose messages you keep deleting knows.
Maybe the bottle hidden where your family cannot see it knows.
Maybe your mirror knows.
Maybe your exhausted body knows because you have treated sleep like weakness and endless productivity like righteousness.
Maybe food has become comfort you run to before God.
Maybe appearance has become an altar.
Maybe the gym has stopped being stewardship and quietly become worship.
Maybe you have been starving yourself for approval.
Maybe you have been feeding an addiction while telling everybody you are fine.
Maybe lust has trained your eyes to consume human beings instead of loving them as people bearing God's image.
Maybe bitterness has been living in your chest so long that you barely remember what peace felt like.
Maybe you have used your hands to hurt.
Your mouth to destroy.
Your sexuality to escape.
Your beauty to manipulate.
Your strength to dominate.
Your body to chase acceptance from people who could never give you what your soul was actually asking for.
And maybe the most frightening part is that you have learned how to worship on Sunday without surrendering any of it.
But listen carefully.
Conviction is not an invitation to run away from Jesus.
It is an invitation to stop running from Him.
There is a difference between biblical conviction and hopeless condemnation.
The enemy would love for your shame to say:
“Hide.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Shame says:
“You ruined everything.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus saves sinners.
Shame says:
“Clean yourself up, then approach God.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
This is why the temple passage must never be separated from the Gospel.
“You were bought with a price.”
The command is built upon redemption.
Paul does not say:
“Make yourself valuable enough for God to purchase.”
He says you were bought.
Grace comes first.
Then grace teaches us how to live.
Paul says elsewhere that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives (Titus 2:11–12).
Biblical grace does not merely forgive the old master.
Grace changes masters.
That is why “my body is a temple” can never honestly mean:
“God wants me attractive.”
Or:
“God promises me perfect health if I behave correctly.”
Scripture promises neither.
Some extraordinarily faithful Christians live with severe illness, disability, chronic pain, scars, infertility, aging bodies, or circumstances they did not choose.
A suffering body is not evidence that someone has failed to honor God.
Paul himself knew physical weakness.
The Christian faith does not worship youth, beauty, muscularity, thinness, health, or longevity.
Jesus Christ is Lord of the healthy body and the hurting body.
The athletic body and the disabled body.
The young body and the aging body.
The body people praise and the body people overlook.
Your worth is not measured by your reflection.
The temple language is fundamentally about belonging.
And belonging changes stewardship.
So yes, Christians should care about what happens to their bodies.
We should resist sexual immorality because Scripture explicitly commands it.
We should refuse drunkenness because Scripture explicitly condemns it.
We should reject gluttony, enslavement to appetites, destructive indulgence, and anything that begins mastering us.
Paul had already said in the same chapter:
“πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν... ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.”
“All things are lawful for me... but I will not be dominated by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12).
That word should haunt every addiction we have renamed “just something I enjoy.”
Dominated.
What can you no longer comfortably say no to?
Pornography?
Alcohol?
Food?
Attention?
Nicotine?
Scrolling?
Sex?
Work?
Appearance?
Entertainment?
Approval?
Exercise?
Even something morally neutral can become spiritually revealing when losing access to it makes us feel as though we cannot function.
The Christian question is not merely:
“Is this technically forbidden?”
Sometimes the more revealing question is:
“Is this becoming my master?”
Because you already have a Master.
And His name is Jesus.
This also means honoring God with your body reaches far beyond avoiding obvious sins.
Your hands belong to Christ.
What could they build?
Whom could they serve?
Whose tears could they wipe away?
Your feet belong to Christ.
Where could they carry the Gospel?
Your mouth belongs to Christ.
Could it stop murdering reputations through gossip and start speaking life?
Your eyes belong to Christ.
Could they learn to see people as souls instead of objects?
Your sexuality belongs to Christ.
Your strength belongs to Christ.
Your weakness belongs to Christ.
Your scars belong to Christ.
Your appetite belongs to Christ.
Your sleep belongs to Christ.
Your work belongs to Christ.
Even the ordinary rhythms nobody applauds can become places of worship.
Romans 12:1 captures the breathtaking scope of this:
“Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.”
A living sacrifice.
That is almost a contradiction.
Sacrifices die.
But this one wakes up tomorrow morning.
And then again the next morning.
And again.
Christian surrender is not merely one dramatic altar call.
Sometimes surrender looks like closing the tab.
Deleting the number.
Walking away from the room.
Asking someone for help.
Going to sleep.
Getting treatment.
Eating with gratitude rather than shame.
Refusing the next drink.
Breaking off the affair.
Confessing the secret.
Choosing purity when nobody would have discovered the compromise.
Looking away.
Getting back up after falling.
Opening Scripture when temptation is screaming louder than truth.
Whispering:
“Jesus, this body belongs to You.”
And perhaps you failed yesterday.
Perhaps you failed an hour ago.
Perhaps you are reading this with the sick feeling that Christians like you are not supposed to struggle with what you are struggling with.
Then remember who wrote these words.
Paul wrote to Corinthians.
Not angels.
Not sanitized religious heroes.
People with baggage.
People surrounded by corruption.
People who had lived in serious sin.
Immediately before this passage, Paul lists forms of unrighteousness and then gives one of the most beautiful sentences ever written to people haunted by their past:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
There is the scandal.
And there is the grace.
Your history can tell the truth about where you have been without being allowed to pronounce the final verdict over who you are in Christ.
Sexual sin does not get the final word.
Addiction does not get the final word.
Your abortion does not get the final word.
Your affair does not get the final word.
Your pornography does not get the final word.
Your drunken nights do not get the final word.
Your self-hatred does not get the final word.
Your years of compromise do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes the cross magnificent.
Repentance is not pretending the wreckage never happened.
Repentance turns around because grace has shown us Someone better.
The Gospel does not tell us that our bodies are irrelevant.
It tells us they have been claimed by a crucified and risen King.
So perhaps the question today is not whether your body looks like a temple.
Maybe the question is whether you are living like it belongs to the King who dwells within you.
You do not need to leave this article promising Jesus that you will become perfect by tomorrow.
You need something deeper.
Surrender.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the appetite.
Bring Him the sexual brokenness.
Bring Him the vanity.
Bring Him the insecurity.
Bring Him the illness.
Bring Him the exhaustion.
Bring Him the scars.
Bring Him the body you love.
Bring Him the body you hate.
Bring Him the parts of your story you still cannot say aloud without trembling.
Repent where repentance is necessary.
Seek forgiveness.
Seek accountability where secrecy has strengthened sin.
Seek appropriate professional help when physical or psychological suffering requires it.
And trust the Savior whose blood is sufficient for repentant sinners.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become better at hiding.
He died and rose so sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, indwelt by His Spirit, and transformed.
Be honest.

And if God has already been restoring an area of your life you thought was beyond repair, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed believer finally believes restoration is possible.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction sounded like yesterday.
Come back when compromise starts negotiating.
Come back when your flesh says, “Just once.”
Come back and remember:
You are not your own. You were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body.
Not as a performance to prove that you love God. Christ alone is our righteousness.
Send it privately to the believer who has been disappearing behind shame.
Send it to the seeker who thinks Christianity is merely a collection of restrictions and needs to see that Christian holiness begins with belonging to Jesus.

Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, building discipleship resources, and carrying the message of Jesus into timelines where despair, temptation, confusion, and spiritual compromise are already preaching every day.
Not because God needs an algorithm.
Because people need the Gospel.
Someone is ashamed of what they did last night.
Someone thinks Jesus has finally become tired of forgiving them.
Someone is enslaved to something they keep calling freedom.
Someone believes their body has been too abused, too used, too sick, too scarred, too old, too broken, or too defiled ever to become part of a holy story again.
Let this reach them.
Because the Gospel has never been about respectable people proving how clean they are.
It is about a holy Savior who receives repentant sinners, washes the guilty, gives His Spirit to His people, and teaches the redeemed to live like they finally understand whose they are.
Your body is not disposable.
Your body is not your god.
Your body is not the measure of your worth.
And for the Christian, your body is no longer merely your private kingdom.
You were bought.
At terrible cost.
By astonishing love.
So glorify God with it.
And when you fail, do not turn failure into permission to keep running.
Run back to Jesus.
Repent.
Confess.
Receive His mercy.
Stand again.
Walk again.
Fight again.
Because sanctification is not the story of Christians who never stumbled.
It is the story of people whom Christ refuses to leave unchanged.
And perhaps this is what you needed to remember before closing this page:
The body carrying the scars of your scandal can still become the place where the grace of Jesus writes your surrender.
